lessons.title: Server Actions: forms, validation, revalidation and security
lessons.summary: How Server Actions work on the wire in Next.js 16, form handling with useActionState and zod, choosing updateTag vs revalidateTag vs refresh, and securing every action as a public endpoint.
lessons.body:
## The core idea A **Server Action** is an async function marked with `'use server'` that the client can call as if it were local. Next.js compiles the call into a **POST request** to the current route. The function runs on the server, and the response carries both the function's return value **and** a freshly rendered RSC payload for the page, when the action revalidated something. One round trip covers the mutation, cache invalidation and updated UI. The convenience hides one fact you must never forget. **Every Server Action is a public HTTP endpoint.** Anyone who can send that POST can call it with any arguments. Rendering the form only for admins protects nothing. The Next.js 16 docs say exactly this in the Server Actions and Data Security guides. ## Defining and invoking actions ```ts // app/posts/actions.ts "use server"; // file-level: every export becomes a Server Action import { z } from "zod"; import { updateTag } from "next/cache"; import { redirect } from "next/navigation"; import { verifySession } from "@/lib/dal"; import { db } from "@/lib/db"; const PostInput = z.object({ title: z.string().trim().min(3).max(120), body: z.string().trim().min(1).max(20_000), }); export type CreatePostState = { errors?: Record; message?: string; values?: { title: string; body: string } }; export async function createPost(_prev: CreatePostState, formData: FormData): Promise { const session = await verifySession(); // 1. authenticate (redirects or throws if missing) const raw = { title: String(formData.get("title") ?? ""), body: String(formData.get("body") ?? "") }; const parsed = PostInput.safeParse(raw); // 2. validate: FormData is untrusted if (!parsed.success) return { errors: parsed.error.flatten().fieldErrors, values: raw }; const post = await db.post.create({ data: { ...parsed.data, authorId: session.userId } }); // 3. mutate updateTag("posts"); // 4. invalidate: read-your-own-writes redirect(`/posts/${post.id}`); // 5. throws a control-flow signal; nothing after it runs } ``` ```tsx // app/posts/new/form.tsx "use client"; import { useActionState } from "react"; import { createPost, type CreatePostState } from "../actions"; export function NewPostForm() { const [state, action, pending] = useActionState(createPost, {}); return (
{state.errors?.title &&

{state.errors.title[0]}

}
keyPoints: A Server Action is a POST to the current route identified by an encrypted action ID
One response carries the return value plus the re-rendered route when you call updateTag, revalidatePath or refresh
Use updateTag for read-your-own-writes; revalidateTag(tag, 'max') is stale-while-revalidate
The framework checks Origin, caps bodies at 1 MB and encrypts IDs; you must authenticate, authorise objects and validate
Actions are dispatched sequentially from the client; use Route Handlers for webhooks and external clients
interview: What actually happens on the network when a Server Action runs?
How do you validate a Server Action form and show field errors without losing input?
After a Server Action, how do you make sure the user sees their own write?
A Server Action receives an item id from the client. What can go wrong and how do you secure it?

check.q: A client calls three Server Actions with Promise.all. How do they run?
options: In parallel, each on its own request
One at a time: Next.js dispatches actions sequentially per client
Only the last one runs
They are merged into a single action
check.why: The Next.js client dispatcher queues actions so each re-rendered tree matches the action that produced it.

check.q: After creating a post in a Server Action, the user is redirected but sees the old list. Which change most directly fixes it?
options: Call revalidateTag('posts', 'max') after redirect()
Add export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'
Call updateTag('posts') before redirect()
Increase the cacheLife stale time
check.why: updateTag expires the tag so the next read waits for fresh data. redirect throws, so anything after it never runs.

check.q: Which protection does Next.js NOT provide for Server Actions automatically?
options: Checking that the caller owns the record being modified
Comparing Origin with Host to block cross-site POSTs
A default 1 MB request body limit
Encrypting action IDs and closed-over variables
check.why: Authorisation is application logic. Re-read the row by id and owner from the session inside every action.

lessons.title: Advanced routing: groups, parallel and intercepting routes
lessons.summary: The App Router boundary tree (layouts, templates, loading and error), route groups, parallel route slots with default.tsx, intercepting routes, and the shareable-URL modal pattern.
lessons.body: ## The core idea The App Router turns folders into a **tree of nested React boundaries**. Each URL segment can contribute a layout (UI that persists), a loading state (a Suspense boundary), an error state (an error boundary), a not-found state and a page. On top of that come three advanced conventions: - **Route groups** `(folder)`: organise routes and share layouts **without** changing the URL. - **Parallel routes** `@slot`: render several independent pages in one layout at the same time, each with its own navigation state. - **Intercepting routes** `(.)`, `(..)`, `(...)`: during client-side navigation, show another route inside the current layout (typically a modal) while the URL changes to the real address. Parallel and intercepting routes together solve a real product problem: a modal with a **shareable URL** that opens as an overlay when you click it in the app, but loads as a full page when someone opens the link directly or refreshes. ## The boundary tree, step by step For `app/dashboard/settings/page.tsx`, Next.js nests the special files of each segment like this (from the project structure docs): ```text app/layout.tsx app/dashboard/layout.tsx
keyPoints: Each segment nests layout, template, error, loading, not-found and page; error and loading wrap what is below, not their own layout
Layouts persist across navigation; templates remount; loading.tsx cannot cover uncached reads in a layout
Route groups share layouts without URL segments; multiple root layouts cause full reloads
Unmatched slots keep state on soft navigation and render default.tsx (or 404) on hard navigation
Intercepting routes plus a @modal slot give a modal with a real, shareable URL
interview: How would you build a photo modal with a shareable URL using parallel and intercepting routes?
Why does a parallel route 404 on refresh, and what is default.tsx for?
What are route groups, and when do multiple root layouts cause a full page reload?
Why doesn't error.tsx catch an error thrown in the layout of the same segment?

check.q: You open /photo/42 directly in a new tab in an app that intercepts that route into a modal. What renders?
options: The modal over an empty page
The modal over the feed
The full photo page, because interception only happens on soft navigation
check.why: Hard navigation never intercepts. The real photo/[id]/page.tsx renders and the modal slot falls back to default.tsx.

check.q: In app/@modal/(..)photo, how is the (..) level counted?
options: By route segments, so the @modal slot folder does not count
By file-system folders, including @modal
From the project root
By the number of layouts above
check.why: Interception matchers count route segments. Slots and groups are not segments.

check.q: A dashboard layout returns role === 'admin' ? admin : user, using two parallel slots. What is the security issue?
options: Parallel routes cannot read cookies
The admin slot is cached publicly
Both slots render on the server, including their data fetches, so authorisation must happen inside each slot
There is none; the condition prevents the admin slot from running
check.why: The conditional only picks what is shown. Every slot at that level executes, so checks belong in the slot or the DAL.

lessons.title: proxy.ts, runtimes and request-time routing
lessons.summary: Next.js 16's proxy.ts (formerly middleware.ts): where it runs, matchers, optimistic auth redirects, rewrites for tenants and experiments, edge vs Node runtimes, and the CVE-2025-29927 lesson.
keyPoints: Next.js 16 renamed middleware.ts to proxy.ts; it runs on Node.js and the runtime cannot be configured
Proxy runs after next.config headers and redirects and before filesystem routes; scope it with a matcher
Use it for optimistic redirects, rewrites and header plumbing, never as the only authorisation layer
Server Actions are POSTs to page routes, so matcher exclusions silently skip them
Edge has fast cold starts but limited APIs and distance from data, which is why Node became the default
interview: Why did Next.js 16 rename middleware.ts to proxy.ts, and what changed?
Edge runtime vs Node.js runtime: what are the trade-offs?
What did CVE-2025-29927 teach about doing auth in middleware?

check.q: A proxy.ts has no matcher and redirects unauthenticated users to /login. What breaks first?
options: Nothing; proxy never runs for static files
Static assets such as _next/static CSS and JS can also be redirected, so even the login page loads unstyled
Only API routes are affected
The build fails
check.why: Without a matcher, Proxy runs on every request, including static files and image optimisation.

check.q: How do you pass a value computed in proxy.ts to a Server Component without exposing it to the browser?
options: NextResponse.next({ headers })
A global variable shared with the page module
A query string parameter on a redirect
NextResponse.next({ request: { headers } }) with a modified copy of the request headers
check.why: Setting request headers forwards them upstream to your app. Passing headers directly sets them on the response sent to the client.

check.q: In Next.js 16, what happens if you export runtime = 'edge' from proxy.ts?
options: Proxy runs on the edge runtime
It is ignored silently
It throws, because the runtime option is not available in Proxy, which always uses Node.js
It falls back to a static export
check.why: Proxy defaults to Node.js and the runtime config is not supported there. The upgrade guide says to keep middleware.ts if you still need edge.

lessons.title: Caching, ISR and running Next.js at scale
lessons.summary: The caching layers in Next.js 16 (Cache Components, 'use cache', cacheLife, tags, ISR, CDN), Vercel vs self-hosting on many instances, and production observability.
lessons.body:
## The core idea Next.js performance at scale comes down to one question: **how often does a request reach your code and your database?** Next.js 16 answers it with stacked caching layers. In 16 the primary model is **Cache Components**: you enable `cacheComponents: true`, mark cacheable work with `'use cache'`, give it a lifetime with `cacheLife` and a name with `cacheTag`, and wrap request-time work in ``. At build time Next.js prerenders a **static shell** of everything it can, which is Partial Prerendering (PPR) as the default. Dynamic holes stream in at request time. The second half of the job is **operational**. The same app behaves differently on Vercel, on one `next start` box, and on ten Kubernetes pods. Caches may be per-instance, encryption keys may differ, deploys may cause version skew, and streaming may be buffered by a proxy. Knowing those failure modes is what separates a senior answer. ## The caching layers, from browser to data ```text Browser 1. Client router cache prefetched / visited RSC payloads, kept for `stale` time (minimum 30 s for 'use cache' content) CDN / reverse proxy 2. HTTP cache honours Cache-Control: static shells and assets are public, dynamic responses are private, no-store Next.js server 3. Static shell / ISR prerendered HTML + payload; revalidated in the background 4. 'use cache' entries function/component outputs keyed by build id + function id + args (in-memory LRU by default; cacheHandlers for Redis etc.) 5. React.cache per-request memoisation (dedupe the same call in one render) Data source 6. Your DB / APIs what all of the above protects ``` **Layer 4 in detail** (from the `use cache` reference): - The cache key combines the **build ID** (or `deploymentId`), a hash of the function's location, and the **serialised arguments**, including variables the function closes over. A new deploy starts with empty `'use cache'` entries. - The function may not call `cookies()`, `headers()` or `searchParams` inside the cached scope, and that applies to helpers it calls too. Read those values outside and pass them in as arguments, which makes them part of the key. - **Runtime persistence depends on the host.** On serverless, in-memory entries usually do not survive between requests (each request may hit a fresh instance). On a long-lived self-hosted server they do. For a shared, durable runtime cache, use `'use cache: remote'` with a configured handler (Redis, KV), which costs a network hop. `'use cache: private'` covers the rare case of caching per-user data that reads cookies directly. **Lifetimes with `cacheLife`.** Each profile has three numbers: `stale` (how long the client uses the entry without asking), `revalidate` (after this, the next request triggers a background refresh) and `expire` (after this with no traffic, the next request waits for fresh data). Built-in profiles: `seconds`, `minutes`, `hours`, `days`, `weeks`, `max`, plus `default`, which is 5 min stale, 15 min revalidate, never expires. Set one explicitly in every cached scope. **On-demand invalidation:** tag with `cacheTag("product:42")`. Then call `updateTag` from a Server Action when the user needs to see their own write immediately, or `revalidateTag(tag, "max")` for stale-while-revalidate from anywhere, such as a CMS webhook Route Handler. ## Code: one page, three kinds of content ```tsx // next.config.ts: cacheComponents: true import { Suspense } from "react"; import { cookies } from "next/headers"; import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from "next/cache"; export default function ProductPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) { return ( <> {/* static: in the shell */} }> {/* cached per id */} Loading your cart...

}> {/* per request: streams */} ); } async function Product({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) { const { id } = await params; return ; } async function ProductBody({ id }: { id: string }) { "use cache"; cacheLife("hours"); cacheTag(`product:${id}`); const p = await db.product.findUnique({ where: { id } }); return ; } async function CartBadge() { const session = (await cookies()).get("session")?.value; // runtime API: must be inside Suspense const count = await getCartCount(session); return {count}; } ``` With Cache Components enabled, the old segment configs (`export const dynamic`, `revalidate`, `fetchCache`) **error** and are replaced by `'use cache'` and `cacheLife`. `unstable_cache` is replaced by `'use cache'`. The docs still point to `unstable_cache` or the `fetch` cache only when an entry must survive across deploys. Use `generateStaticParams` to prerender known IDs at build time. **ISR** is the same idea at the page level. A prerendered page is served from cache and regenerated in the background after its revalidate window, or when its tags are invalidated. For pages, Next.js sends `Cache-Control: s-maxage=, stale-while-revalidate` so that a CDN can hold them. Dynamically rendered pages get `private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate`, so a CDN never caches personal HTML. ## Vercel vs self-hosting **On Vercel**, the platform handles the hard parts: a globally shared ISR and data cache, tag invalidation across regions, the CDN in front, streaming, image optimisation, skew protection between deployments, and preview deployments. You pay with platform limits and usage pricing. **Self-hosting** (`next start`, Docker with `output: "standalone"`, or a platform adapter) gives you every feature, including Proxy, ISR, streaming and Cache Components, but these become your job. From the self-hosting guide: | Concern | What goes wrong | Fix | | --- | --- | --- | | ISR / page cache | stored on each instance's disk and memory, so pods disagree; ephemeral disks lose it | custom `cacheHandler` (Redis, S3) and `cacheMaxMemorySize: 0` | | `'use cache'` entries | in-memory per instance | `cacheHandlers` + `'use cache: remote'` | | Tag invalidation | `revalidateTag` on pod A does not reach pod B | implement `refreshTags()` in the handler to sync tag state from shared storage | | Server Actions | each build or instance has a different key, so "Failed to find Server Action" | the same `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (base64 AES key) at build time | | Rolling deploys | old clients request missing chunks or old action IDs | `deploymentId`, so Next.js detects skew and does a hard navigation | | Build IDs | rebuilding per environment gives different IDs | build once, promote the artefact; or `generateBuildId` | | Streaming | nginx or the load balancer buffers responses, so PPR loses its TTFB win | `X-Accel-Buffering: no`, and a load balancer that supports chunked transfer | | Images | optimiser CPU and memory on your servers | size the pods, or use a loader for an image CDN | | Shutdown | in-flight requests and `after()` callbacks cut off | handle SIGTERM with a 10-30 s drain period | ## Observability - **Tracing:** add `instrumentation.ts` with `export function register()`. The quickest setup is `registerOTel({ serviceName: "web" })` from `@vercel/otel`. Next.js emits OpenTelemetry spans for requests, rendering, route handlers and fetches. Export them over OTLP to any backend (Grafana Tempo, Honeycomb, Datadog). - **Server errors:** `export async function onRequestError(err, request, context)` in `instrumentation.ts` gets every server error with route and render context. Forward it to Sentry or your logger. Production errors show users a generic message with a `digest`, so log the digest and you can join a user report to the server stack trace. - **Client:** `useReportWebVitals` (or `instrumentation-client.ts`) sends real-user LCP, INP and CLS to analytics. Field data beats Lighthouse. - **Cache visibility:** log cache hits and misses in your cache handler, and alert when the DB QPS per request rises. That is how a broken tag or a key that is too fine-grained shows up. ## Trade-offs and when not to cache - Personalised, fast-changing data (balances, carts, inventory at checkout) should stay request-time. Show it in a Suspense hole rather than caching it per user. - Fine-grained keys (a whole `searchParams` object, a timestamp argument) give a near-zero hit rate and fill memory. - `'use cache: remote'` adds a network round trip and cost to every lookup. Use it where the origin is expensive, not by default. - Self-hosting saves money at scale but costs engineering time on every item in the table above. ## Common mistakes and debugging - Reading `cookies()` inside a cached function. It errors, sometimes only at runtime under `next start`. - Expecting in-memory `'use cache'` to absorb traffic on serverless. - Calling `revalidateTag` on a multi-pod deployment without a shared handler, so some users see stale pages. - Using a different encryption key per instance. - Forgetting a `` around runtime data, which triggers the blocking-route error in development. - Putting a CDN in front without respecting `Vary` and the RSC headers, so HTML and payload variants get mixed up. - **Debugging:** run `next build` and read the route output, which marks static, partially prerendered and dynamic routes. Inspect `Cache-Control` and `x-nextjs-cache`-style response headers, and follow the OpenTelemetry trace for slow requests. ## In the interview **What they probe:** whether you can name the layers, explain how Next 16's Cache Components differ from older ISR configs, and run Next.js on your own infrastructure without stale caches or broken actions. **60-second answer outline:** 1. The layers are client router cache, CDN, static shell and ISR, `'use cache'` entries, per-request `React.cache`, then the DB. 2. In Next 16, `cacheComponents` plus `'use cache'`, `cacheLife` and `cacheTag` replace `dynamic`, `revalidate` and `fetchCache`. Runtime data goes behind Suspense, and the static shell is prerendered (PPR). 3. Invalidate with `updateTag` for read-your-own-writes, or `revalidateTag(tag, "max")` for stale-while-revalidate. 4. Self-hosting needs a shared cache handler with tag sync, a stable action encryption key, a `deploymentId` for skew, unbuffered streaming and graceful shutdown. 5. Observe with OpenTelemetry via `instrumentation.ts`, `onRequestError` with digests, and real-user Web Vitals. **Follow-ups to expect:** Why does my cached function run on every request on serverless? What happens to cache entries on deploy? How do you invalidate a product page when the CMS changes it? How would you run this on Kubernetes?
keyPoints: Layers: client router cache, CDN, static shell and ISR, 'use cache' entries, React.cache, then the data source
cacheComponents with 'use cache', cacheLife and cacheTag replaces dynamic, revalidate and fetchCache segment configs
In-memory 'use cache' entries rarely survive on serverless; use 'use cache: remote' with a handler for shared caching
Multi-instance self-hosting needs a shared cache handler with tag sync, one encryption key, deploymentId and unbuffered streaming
Observe with OpenTelemetry in instrumentation.ts, onRequestError with error digests, and real-user Web Vitals

check.q: A function marked 'use cache' calls cookies() through a helper. What happens?
options: The cookie value becomes part of the cache key automatically
The cache is silently disabled for that function
It works only in development
It errors, because request-time APIs are not allowed anywhere in the cached call stack
check.why: Read cookies outside the cached scope and pass the value as an argument, which then becomes part of the key.

check.q: You run four Next.js pods. revalidateTag on pod A works, but users on other pods still see stale pages. What is missing?
options: A shared cache handler that implements tag coordination (refreshTags) across instances
A larger cacheMaxMemorySize
export const dynamic = 'force-static'
A shorter cacheLife stale time
check.why: By default each instance has its own cache and invalidates only locally. Shared storage plus tag sync fixes it.

check.q: Which response header does Next.js set for dynamically rendered pages to keep CDNs from caching personal HTML?
options: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate
private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate
Vary: Cookie only
check.why: Immutable caching is for hashed assets and s-maxage for ISR pages. Dynamic responses are marked private and no-store.
